T2A01: On 2 meters the standard repeater offset is 600 kHz: the repeater listens 600 kHz above or below where it transmits. For example, a repeater transmitting on 146.940 MHz typically listens on 146.340 MHz (minus offset). 5 MHz is the 70 cm offset.
T2A02: 146.520 MHz is the national 2-meter FM simplex calling frequency. 446.000 MHz is the 70 cm calling frequency, and 432.100 MHz is a 70 cm SSB/CW weak-signal calling frequency.
T2A03: On 70 cm (420-450 MHz) the standard repeater offset is 5 MHz. Memory tip: the higher band gets the bigger offset: 2 m = 600 kHz, 70 cm = 5 MHz.
T2A04: To call a specific station on a repeater, say their call sign, then identify with yours (for example, 'W1AW, this is KF1XXX'). 'Break break' is reserved for urgent or emergency traffic, and CQ is a general call to anyone, which is uncommon on repeaters.
T2A05: When answering a CQ, give their call sign first, then yours, as in 'W1AW, this is KF1XXX.' This tells the calling station that you are answering them and who you are.
T2A06: The standard general call on simplex/HF phone is 'CQ CQ CQ, this is KF1XXX,' repeated a few times, then listen for a reply. An unmodulated carrier is never an acceptable way to call, and QTC refers to message traffic.
T2A07: Repeater offset is the difference between the repeater's transmit (output) and receive (input) frequencies. Your radio automatically transmits on the input and listens on the output when you set the offset.
T2A08: CQ means 'calling any station.' It is a general invitation for anyone to answer. It does not refer to contests or audio quality.
T2A09: On a repeater, the customary way to announce that you are available is to give your call sign followed by 'listening' (or 'monitoring'). Calling CQ on a repeater is generally not done.
T2A10: A band plan is a voluntary agreement among amateurs (often published by the ARRL) about which modes and activities happen in which part of a band, beyond what the FCC rules require. Following it helps avoid conflicts, such as SSB operators interfering with weak-signal CW.
T2A11: Simplex means transmitting and receiving on the same frequency, with stations taking turns, and no repeater in between. Full duplex is transmitting and receiving at the same time on different frequencies.
T2B01: The reverse function swaps your transmit and receive frequencies, so you listen on the repeater's input. If you can hear the other station directly on the input, you might be close enough to switch to simplex and free up the repeater.
T2B02: CTCSS (Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System, also called PL tone) is a sub-audible tone sent with your voice. Many repeaters will only open their squelch when they hear the correct tone. DTMF is the touch-tone keypad signaling.
T2B03: In a linked repeater network, repeaters are connected (by radio or internet) so that a signal received by one is retransmitted by all of them. This allows coverage over a wide area.
T2B04: If you can hear a repeater but can't get into it, check that your offset is correct and that you are sending the correct CTCSS tone or DCS code. Any one of these mistakes will prevent the repeater from hearing you.
T2B05: Talking too loudly (or too close to the mic) causes over-deviation. Many repeaters and receivers cut out or distort when the FM deviation exceeds the expected width. The fix is to back off from the microphone or speak more softly.
T2B06: DTMF (Dual-Tone Multi-Frequency) is touch-tone signaling, which sends two simultaneous tones for each key. It is used to send control commands to repeaters (for example, to turn on a link).
T2B07: On DMR digital repeaters, you join a talkgroup by programming your radio with that talkgroup's ID number, usually by loading a code plug. No registration with the frequency coordinator is involved.
T2B08: No one owns a frequency. When two stations interfere with each other, they should work it out cooperatively (negotiate), and one may move. Being first does not legally give preemptive rights, although courtesy usually favors the station already there.
T2B09: Simplex channels let stations that are close enough to hear each other talk directly, leaving the repeater free for stations that actually need its range.
T2B10: QRM means interference from other stations (man-made). QRN is natural noise (static), QTH is location, and QSB is fading. Memory tip: 'M' for man-made, 'N' for natural.
T2B11: QSY means 'change frequency' (as in 'let's QSY to 146.55'). QSL is 'I acknowledge receipt,' QRZ is 'who is calling me?', and QRU is 'I have nothing for you.'
T2B12: A DMR color code works like CTCSS for DMR: it is a number (0-15) that must match the repeater's code for your transmission to be accepted. It lets multiple repeaters share a frequency.
T2B13: Squelch mutes the receiver's audio when no signal is present, so you don't hear constant noise (hiss) between transmissions. When a signal strong enough to exceed the threshold arrives, audio is unmuted.
T2B14: In DMR, a talkgroup is an identifier used to organize traffic. You only hear the talkgroups you've selected, so you aren't bothered by other conversations on the same network.
T2C01: FCC Part 97 rules always apply to amateur stations, even during an emergency, and even when working with RACES, ARES, or FEMA. Those organizations operate within the FCC rules, not outside them.
T2C02: The Net Control Station (NCS) calls the net to order, takes check-ins, and directs which stations transmit and when. Checking licenses or setting the net schedule is not part of the NCS's typical job.
T2C03: Spelling unusual words using a standard phonetic alphabet (Alfa, Bravo, Charlie...) ensures that the receiving station copies them correctly. This is standard practice in message handling.
T2C04: RACES (Radio Amateur Civil Emergency Service) is an FCC Part 97 amateur radio service for civil defense communications during national or local emergencies. It does not involve CB radio.
T2C05: In nets, 'traffic' means formal messages being passed between stations, such as radiograms. A traffic net exists to relay these messages.
T2C06: ARES (Amateur Radio Emergency Service, sponsored by the ARRL) is a group of licensed amateurs who have voluntarily registered their qualifications and equipment for public service communications duty. It is not a military organization or a licensing course.
T2C07: In a directed net, you transmit only when the net control station directs you to, unless you have emergency traffic. This keeps the net orderly. You don't give your address or log each transmission.
T2C08: Winlink is a worldwide radio email system. Each user's email address is based on their call sign (for example, KF1XXX@winlink.org). It is heavily used for emergency communications.
T2C09: In an emergency involving the immediate safety of human life or protection of property, when no other means of communication is available, any amateur may use any means necessary, including operating outside their license privileges.
T2C10: The preamble of a formal message (radiogram) contains the information needed to track the message: number, precedence, station of origin, check, place of origin, time and date. The recipient's address appears in a separate section.
T2C11: The 'check' in a radiogram header is the count of words (or word equivalents) in the message text. The receiving station uses it to verify that nothing was lost in transmission.
T2C12: RACES requires certification (enrollment) by a civil defense organization. ARES, SKYWARN, and MARS have their own membership processes but do not require civil defense certification.
